newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada voters deserting Quebec separatists - poll.
newsitem.headline: Canada voters deserting Quebec separatists - poll.

text.p: The separatist Bloc Quebec party is losing voter support in Canada's Quebec province, while the ruling Liberals and the Progressive Conservative Party have surged, an opinion poll showed on Saturday.
It found that for the first time since the last election, in 1993, more Quebec voters who had decided which party to support said they intended to vote for the Liberals than for the Bloc Quebec.
Groupe Leger & Leger took the poll for the Globe and Mail and Le Journal de Montreal newspapers ahead of the June 2 federal election.

It found that 38.8 percent of Quebec voters who had decided said they intended to vote for the Liberals, up from 36.9 percent in a similar poll two weeks earlier. The number intending to back the Bloc Quebec fell to 37.1 percent from 43.1 percent.

Much of the drop reflected a gain for the Conservatives. A total of 19.8 percent of voters who had decided said they preferred the Conservatives, a rise from 14.6 percent. Overall, 20.4 percent of those questioned were undecided.
The poll surveyed 1,008 voters and had a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points 19 times out of 20. It was taken over four days during the past week, starting on Tuesday.

Quebec's independence drive turned into a major issue late this week, the second week of the election campaign, as the Liberals under Prime Minister Jean Chretien accused the separatists of deceiving Quebeckers about their plans.

Chretien, who is from Quebec, has fought efforts by the Bloc Quebec to take the province out of Canada. The federalist camp narrowly lost a referendum on the question in 1995, and another referendum is widely expected within the next few years.

A Quebec newspaper reported this week that former Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau had planned to declare unilateral independence immediately if the separatists had won the 1995 referendum, contrary to public promises to move slowly and negotiate an arrangement maintaining many links with Canada.

Parizeau denied the report but not before it caused confusion in the separatist camp and provoked harsh rhetoric from the Liberals and other unity supporters. This was not the first stumble for the Bloc Quebec's election campaign, which political analysts have called poorly handled.

The Leger & Leger poll found that Conservative leader Jean Charest, also a Quebecker, was the most popular party leader in the province, with 31.9 percent support. Chretien was preferred by 24.7 percent of voters, and Bloc Quebec leader Gilles Duceppe garnered 22.3 percent.
Those surveyed said that the Conservatives had run the best campaign so far, with the Liberals next and the Bloc Quebec third.

Despite the erosion in support, the Bloc Quebec still appears likely to win at least 40 parliamentary seats, pollster Jean-Marc Leger told the Globe. He said results of the poll were consistent over four days of polling, suggesting that the controversy over Parizeau's plans had little immediate impact.
